li.a: Página/12: La Masacre de Ezeiza y la Triple A
Perfil, from Télam: Investigan si la AAA actuó en masacre de Ezeiza
El Historiador: La masacre de Ezeiza (excerpts from Felipe Pigna, Lo pasado pensado)
Perfil: Qué fue la masacre de Ezeiza
La Izquierda Diario: La Masacre de Ezeiza, bautismo de fuego de la derecha peronista
La Nación: Hace 25 años, la masacre de Ezeiza enlutaba a la Argentina
Horacio Verbitsky, Ezeiza (Editorial Contrapunto, 1985), online text

content.p: On 20 June 1973 Argentina expected its biggest political celebration. Juan Domingo Perón, the former president, was flying home after 18 years of exile, and about two million people, according to the historian Felipe Pigna's collection of interviews, gathered in the woods near Ezeiza airport to see him. Instead the day became the worst tragedy at a public event in Argentine history, in the words of a La Nación writer 25 years later. Gunfire broke out around the stage built beside the highway, the crowd stampeded, and Perón's aircraft was sent to a military base instead.

The figure repeated most often is 13 dead and 365 injured. La Nación's 1998 retrospective gave 16 dead and more than 200 injured. Perfil, in 2021, said the toll was estimated at 13 dead and more than 300 injured, but that the exact figures are unknown. No court has convicted anyone of the killings. The case was shelved in 1983. In 2007 its file was sent to a federal judge who wanted to know whether the same people were behind it and the death squad known as the Triple A.
content.h2: A movement at war with itself
content.p: To understand why a welcome turned into a shooting, begin with Peronism's split. Perón's party had been banned since he was overthrown in 1955. Perfil describes how it survived that ban at a price: a struggle for control between young left-wing organisations and the right-wing union leadership, which turned violent. On 25 May 1973 Héctor Cámpora, the Peronist candidate, took office as president, in what El Historiador calls the first election without bans since 1955. La Nación recalls his campaign slogan, which put Cámpora in government and Perón in power.

The left of the movement, the Tendencia Revolucionaria including the Montoneros, saw Cámpora's inauguration as a victory, Perfil says. His government freed political prisoners the same day, according to La Izquierda Diario, and young Peronists gained influence in provincial governments. Union leaders were uneasy. That outlet says they warned the exiled Perón about infiltrators and the advance of the left in the unions.

La Izquierda Diario, whose account is openly from the left, argues that Perón leaned first on one side and then on the other, as it suited him, and had struck a deal with the union and right-wing groups before he came home. It names the committee that organised the Ezeiza reception: the CGT leader Lorenzo Miguel, Norma Kennedy for the women's branch, Osinde, who was then secretary for sport and tourism, and Juan Manuel Abal Medina, the movement's secretary general, whom it describes as the only member with good relations with the Peronist left. The fight at Ezeiza, in Perfil's telling, began over where each faction would stand near the stage.

La Nación's reconstruction, based on its own edition of 21 June 1973, starts at three in the morning. A group of young people chanted a slogan for a socialist homeland, and others answered with one for a Peronist homeland. Shooting followed, and three people were hit. Later the guards of the official stage, under retired colonel Osinde, traded blows with young people trying to get closer to it.

Near two in the afternoon, the paper reported, groups carrying banners of the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias, the Montoneros and the ERP arrived from a nearby road. La Nación wrote that from the stage the shooting was done with carbines, sawn-off shotguns, machine guns and pistols, while the attackers were using long guns with telescopic sights, snipers in trees. The paper's account, though, also records that the Peronist Youth and the Sindical Youth had been responding to an aggression that seemed to come from a wood about 150 metres away. Its description is of a battle between rival factions.

The other version holds that it was an ambush. El Historiador's summary of the event says that when the FAR and Montonero columns tried to enter the area, men loyal to Osinde fired on them from the stage. La Izquierda Diario says about three thousand armed men under Osinde and the police chief, General Iñiguez, had been positioned near the stage and had orders to shoot if the columns came into the first 300 metres, reserved for people brought by the unions. It says the union-organised crowd numbered fewer than two hundred thousand. Figures like these come from that outlet and not from the court record.

La Nación adds scenes that show the confusion. The actor Leonardo Favio, who was conducting the event on the loudspeakers, asked for calm while carrying a pistol. Doves were released as a symbol of peace as snipers fell. The crowd chanted that it was Peronist, rejecting both of the rival labels, and ran for cover, and people were trampled. The wounded went to hospitals in Ezeiza, Lanús, Haedo and Buenos Aires.

A journalist who covered the day, writing in La Nación in 1998, remembered Montonero columns marching along the highway organised like military columns and chanting declarations of war rather than simple slogans, and said the first shots he heard hit the trees nearby. Mario Firmenich, the Montonero leader, told Pigna that his movement had come to show Perón its mass strength, with giant banners 50 metres long reading "Montoneros". He said they left Ezeiza without knowing what had happened because everything took place behind the stage, and that he sometimes thought the massacre had not been premeditated. The writer Miguel Bonasso told the same interviewer there had been no confrontation at all: his side had been disarmed, and what happened was murder, a massacre. Martín Caparrós said some Montoneros were armed but far fewer than their opponents.

Perón's Aerolíneas Argentinas flight from Madrid carried a large party that included President Cámpora. It came down at the Morón air base. La Nación says that was at 16:50; La Izquierda Diario says the stage announcer was still promising Perón's arrival at 16:20, and the plane landed minutes later. The delegation was told of serious incidents at Ezeiza. The organisers said the Morón landing was improvised because of the situation around Ezeiza. La Izquierda Diario disputes that, claiming it had been known for hours that Perón was expected at Morón, and quotes the writer Miguel Bonasso as saying that an official of José López Rega, the social welfare minister, had told him before the event not to bother going because Perón would never arrive there.

Cámpora spoke to the nation by radio once he landed. La Nación reports him saying that Perón was perfectly well and that elements opposed to the country had tried to distort the event. That night, at his residence in Olivos, Perón said he had not landed at Ezeiza because the runways had been invaded and he feared causing personal tragedies, without blaming anyone, the paper says. His more political speech came the next night, when he said the country had a revolution to carry out but that it had to be one of peaceful reconstruction, costing the life of not a single Argentine.

La Izquierda Diario quotes the same broadcast of 21 June at greater length and reads it differently. It points out that he did not condemn the attacks and told people trying to "infiltrate" popular and state bodies that they were on the wrong road. Firmenich likewise said Perón put the blame on the left; Caparrós said Perón condemned the Montoneros as the authors of the confrontation, which in his view they were not.

The state never produced a trustworthy count. La Nación wrote in 1998 that state bodies had never published the true balance of dead and wounded. Horacio Verbitsky, a journalist who reconstructed the day in his 1985 book Ezeiza, wrote that there were no official reports on the victims and that none of the parties made up for the lack. He identified 13 dead. Three, he wrote, belonged to the Montoneros or their youth groups: Horacio Simona, Antonio Quispe and Hugo Oscar Lanvers. One, Army captain Roberto Máximo Chavarri, was part of the stage security organised by Osinde. He did not know who the other nine were, though he gave their names.

The injured are harder still. Verbitsky says the lists were drawn up by different federal, provincial and municipal bodies from hospitals and police stations, were incomplete, and spelled the same name several ways. Exact reconstruction is impossible, he wrote, but he proposed a minimum estimate. A Buenos Aires provincial intelligence service listed 102 identified injured on 22 June. A police report of 21 June, signed by chief inspector Julio Méndez, gave the same number and added 205 unidentified at the Ezeiza polyclinic. A provincial health office counted another 17 at the Haedo surgery hospital. These sit below the 365 usually quoted, which the sources do not reconcile.

Named in connection with the organisation, in an account the court later reviewed, were the Concentración Nacional Universitaria, armed members of the Movimiento Nueva Argentina, union bodyguards, Alberto Brito Lima's Comando de Organización with Norma Kennedy, and Osinde's old military guard. Página/12 reported in 2007 that these names appeared in two books considered in the Oyarbide inquiry, by Marcelo Larraqui and Juan Gasparini. Osinde was described as one of the people regarded as chiefly responsible, though Página/12 noted that legally the link between the massacre and the Triple A had not been shown. These are accusations drawn from books and journalism. The pages opened for this account do not report a trial or conviction of Osinde or of any of the others named.

Verbitsky also describes how the aftermath was fought over in government. Cámpora spent more than three hours going over the information with ministers, union leaders and police chiefs, and Osinde brought six documents to that discussion. Verbitsky says the interior minister, Esteban Righi, and Osinde headed the two sides, which gave opposed accounts of the cause. In his "Informe sintético", Osinde recalled asking before the event that security forces repress any attempt at disturbance severely, and Righi objecting to the word "repress". Verbitsky also records a story in the press, which El Economista attributed to a member of Osinde's security, that the detainees held at the hotel had carried body armour and telescopic rifles to attack Perón.

La Izquierda Diario says prisoners were beaten and cut at the stage and that the Hotel Internacional was used to torture them. It also claims ambulances of the Ministry of Social Welfare carried weapons, and lists the arms. Larraqui's book, summarised by Página/12, makes a similar statement about ambulances. The 2007 reports said the judge wanted to establish whether the ambulances had been used to send weapons to Ezeiza.

Cámpora lasted 49 days; La Izquierda Diario says he resigned on 13 July and was replaced by Raúl Lastiri, López Rega's son-in-law, until Perón took office in October. Perfil dates the creation of the Triple A to 21 November 1973, by López Rega, and calls Ezeiza a prelude to it. Judge Oyarbide's inquiry, as Página/12 reported, treats that month's bombing of the car of the Radical senator Hipólito Solari Yrigoyen as the start of the organisation's activity, not Ezeiza. La Izquierda Diario's author takes the opposite view and likens Ezeiza to a serpent's egg.

The criminal case had a slow history. Página/12 reports that in 1983 Judge José Nicasio Dibur provisionally dismissed the accused at the request of the prosecutor Julio César Strassera. That June, a former police inspector, Rodolfo Peregrino Fernández, gave testimony to the Argentine human rights commission in Madrid, chaired by Eduardo Luis Duhalde, and confirmed it to the United Nations in Geneva. He described parapolice groups and named López Rega and others in setting up the Triple A.

In February 2007 Judge Oyarbide asked the Lomas de Zamora court for the Ezeiza file, which Perfil and Télam said ran to just under 2,000 pages. He and the federal prosecutor Eduardo Taiano meant to compare the names in both cases. Página/12 pointed to the former policemen Rodolfo Almirón and Juan Ramón Morales, whom Oyarbide had processed in January over the Triple A, and whose band, according to Verbitsky's book, was one of the groups that acted on 20 June with its own weapons. The pages opened do not report what came of the comparison.

La Nación, a quarter of a century on, was struck that hardly anyone marked the anniversary. It argued that the episode was too serious to be forgotten and that the Puente 12 at Ezeiza remained a symbol of the violence Argentina had known.
